L0@P0: SPECTRAL-SPATIAL JOINT SPARSITY UNMIXING OF HYPERSPECTRAL DATA USING
L1@P0: OVERCOMPLETE DICTIONARIES
L2@P0: J. Bieniarz, E. Aguilera, X. X. Zhu, R. Muller, U. Heiden, P. Reinartz ¨
L3@P0: German Aerospace Center (DLR), Oberpfaffenhofen, 82234 Wessling, Germany.
L4@P0: ABSTRACT
L5@P0: Sparse spectral unmixing can be modeled as a linear combination of endmembers contained in an overcomplete dictionary weighted by the corresponding sparse abundance vector. This method exploits the fact that there is only a small
L6@P0: number of endmembers inside a pixel compared to the overcomplete endmember spectral dictionary. Since the information contained in hyperspectral pixels is often spatially correlated, in this work we propose to jointly estimate the sparse
L7@P0: abundance vectors of neighboring hyperspectral pixels within
L8@P0: a local window exploiting joint sparsity with common and
L9@P0: noncommon endmembers. To demonstrate the efficiency of
L10@P0: our framework, we perform experiments using both simulated
L11@P0: and real hyperspectral data.
L12@P0: Index Terms— Spectral unmixing, joint sparsity, overcomplete spectral dictionary.
L13@P0: 1. INTRODUCTION
L14@P0: A common approach to model pixels of hyperspectral images
L15@P0: (HSI) exploits a linear mixing of spectral signatures referred
L16@P0: to as endmembers. These signatures correspond to the spectra
L17@P0: of pure materials, which can be obtained from field/laboratory
L18@P0: spectrometer measurements [1] or determined from the data
L19@P0: by exploiting pixels known to contain a single material. The
L20@P0: basic linear mixing model will be assumed to be given by
L21@P0: yj = Axj + εj (1)

L33@P0: m is a perturbation
L34@P0: term that captures any modeling errors and noise contributions [1]. Thus, given yj and A, the goal is to recover the
L35@P0: unknown vector xj .
L36@P0: Traditional inversion techniques include the method of
L37@P0: least squares (LS), nonnegative least squares (NNLS) [1],
L38@P0: and fully-constrained least squares (FCLS) [3]. While NNLS

L41@P0: ensures the LS criterion is restricted to nonnegative abundances, FCLS additionally enforces that the elements of the
L42@P0: abundance vector sum to one. Although often employed,
L43@P0: these techniques are limited to overdetermined mixing models and thus require a preselection of endmembers based on
L44@P0: a priori knowledge [1]. In contrast, recent sparsity-based
L45@P0: unmixing algorithms have been shown to be able to deal
L46@P0: with the underdetermined case [2, 4, 5]. In essence, these
L47@P0: techniques exploit the fact that—assuming a suitable spatial
L48@P0: resolution—only few endmembers contribute to yj . In other
L49@P0: words, high-resolution imaging renders the vector xj sparse.
L50@P0: Accordingly, recovery of abundances is usually achieved by
L51@P0: solving optimization problems such as basis pursuit denoising (BPDN) [6] or the least absolute shrinkage and selection
L52@P0: operator (LASSO) [7].
L53@P0: Spatial contextual homogeneity is exploited by applying
L54@P0: an alternative joint sparsity model (JSM) originally introduced in [8]. In this setting, every vector xj will be recovered
L55@P0: together with a small number of neighboring abundance vectors selected by means of a window centered on the jth spatial
L56@P0: position. The basic inputs to the algorithm are then multiple
L57@P0: neighboring pixels yj (hereinafter referred to as looks) as well
L58@P0: as a dictionary A. Thus, the goal will be to take advantage
L59@P0: of the fact that the ensemble of unknown vectors exhibit both
L60@P0: common endmembers and abundances. As will be shown,
L61@P0: this approach also allows for capturing their noncommon
L62@P0: endmembers. Finally, the applicability of JSM will be validated by comparing it with BPDN, NNLS using both real and
L63@P0: simulated data.

L228@P1: 3. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
L229@P1: We have tested our algorithm using simulated and real hyperspectral data. For the simulation experiment, we used 90 manmade materials, vegetation, and soil spectra selected from
L230@P1: the USGS spectral dictionary [10], merged with endmembers
L231@P1: from a DLR roof-material dictionary containing 39 endmembers into one spectral dictionary A with finally m = 129 endmembers. After discarding noisy and water-absorption bands,
L232@P1: each spectrum in the dictionary exhibits n = 96 bands.
L233@P1: 3.1. Simulated Scenario
L234@P1: In order to assess the performance of the MLJSR algorithm
L235@P1: with hyperspectral data using the dictionary A, we simulated
L236@P1: 10000 joint YL pixel ensembles each with L = 4 pixels. The
L237@P1: pixels y1, ..., y4 form a mixture of 2, 3, 3, and 4 endmembers,
L238@P1: respectively, and share 2 common endmembers. The common and noncommon endmembers were randomly selected
L239@P1: from the dictionary A and the abundances for all pixels were
L240@P1: also randomly chosen with the sum to one restriction. The
L241@P1: abundance of each common endmember was at least 10%.
L242@P1: Additionally, the simulated pixels were contaminated with
L243@P1: white noise to achieve a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 25,
L244@P1: 30, 40, 50, and 60 dB, respectively. The SNR, signal-toreconstruction error (SRE) are defined as in [9]. The errors
L245@P1: are calculated for pixel y4 in all simulated YL, as the most
L246@P1: mixed pixels contain 2 common and 2 noncommon endmembers. Fig. 2 presents results for the simulated pixels experiment using both MLJSR and BPDN method. The function of
L247@P1: mean SRE for 10000 simulated pixels with different SNR is
L248@P1: plotted. The proposed MLJSR outperforms NNLS as well as
L249@P1: BPDN for all tested noise conditions.

L292@P2: For the experiment with real data we used a hyperspectral scene acquired over Dresden, Germany, with the airborne
L293@P2: sensor HyMap [11]. The scene with originally 126 spectral
L294@P2: channels was reduced to 96. The image has been atmospherically and geometrically corrected with a ground resolution of
L295@P2: 4 m. The window size for MLJSR was L = 9 where the unmixed pixel yi,j was in the center of the window. By sliding
L296@P2: the window over the image each pixel was processed, i.e., we
L297@P2: used measurements of all 9 pixels to get a reliable unmixing
L298@P2: only for the central pixel.
L299@P2: We have tested both MLJSR and BPDN with 10 λ parameters arranged in the range from e
L300@P2: −9
L301@P2: to e. In order to select
L302@P2: the best reconstruction, we have overlapped all unmixing results on the high resolution image and empirically selected
L303@P2: the λ parameter which provided the best results according to
L304@P2: our knowledge. The qualitative comparison of the unmixing
L305@P2: results is presented in Fig. 3. These results were computed using NNLS (right column), both BPDN (middle column) and
L306@P2: MLJSR (left column) with λ = 0.13. The MLJSR algorithm
L307@P2: in comparison to BPDN and NNLS results in smoother transitions from one material to another which indicates better
L308@P2: recovery of mixed pixels with small abundances for selected
L309@P2: materials. This benefits from the joint recovery of neighboring pixels.
L310@P2: 4. CONCLUSION
L311@P2: In this paper we have proposed a multi-look joint sparse
L312@P2: reconstruction for sparse spectral unmixing. The proposed
L313@P2: model takes advantage of the neighboring information by
L314@P2: means of joint approximation of abundances in a sliding window and especially a joint approximation of common endmembers. Compared to the standard sparse BPDN or NNLS
L315@P2: method, experiments with simulated data demonstrate that
L316@P2: the proposed method restores abundances for pixels sharing
L317@P2: common endmembers more accurately in terms of the SRE
L318@P2: measure. The qualitative analysis of the results on HyMAP
L319@P2: image shows the MLJSR approach to be competitive with
L320@P2: respect to BPDN and NNLS methods and visually show more
L321@P2: consistent results. As future work, we propose to address
L322@P2: further tests on real hyperspectral data including quantitative
L323@P2: analysis. Additionally, the MLJSR can be extended to a more
L324@P2: complex design, e.g. incorporating not only common endmembers in the whole window but also shared endmembers
L325@P2: between singular pixels in the window.
